newsitem.title: PERU: Peru economy set for sustained growth - Fujimori.
newsitem.headline: Peru economy set for sustained growth - Fujimori.

text.p: President Alberto Fujimori said Wednesday the Peruvian economy is on course for sustained growth fueled by private investment and the government's welfare and public works expenditures.
"Starting this year the rate of growth will be five percent based on private investment and social spending," Fujimori told a conference of Central Bank officials from the Americas and Spain.

After a longer-than-expected slowdown last year, the economic performance in the first months of 1997 indicates the government will reach its gross domestic product growth target of five percent this year, according to analysts.
The economy grew 4.1 percent year-on-year in February compared with 4.2 percent growth in the year to February 1996, according to latest government figures.
The government has also agreed with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) a growth target of above six percent in 1998.

Speaking on Wednesday, the second anniversary of his re-election in 1995, Fujimori said that since he took power in 1990 the Peruvian economy had become stable due to the administration's fight against runaway inflation and its tight fiscal spending.
Fujimori described Peru before and after he came to power as two different countries.
"One was the country that spent what it did not have and the other is a country that invests in its future," the president said.

Economic stability had attracted private investment that helped the Central Reserve Bank net international reverses climb to a current $9.3 billion after the country had what amounted to "negative" reserves in 1990, Fujimori said.
Peru's net international reserves were $9.173 billion at the end of March, according to the central bank's latest figures.
The government estimates the country's net international reserves will rise above $10 billion by mid-1998.
